mainEntity.name: Is it normal for a dental crown to feel bigger than my original tooth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, it is very common for a crown to feel larger or bulkier than your natural tooth in the first days after placement. This is because your mouth is highly sensitive to even small changes in shape or contour. The tongue and cheeks are particularly adept at detecting differences. In most cases, this sensation fades as the mouth adapts. If the crown still feels noticeably wide or uncomfortable after two weeks, it is worth booking a review appointment with your dentist so the fit and bite can be assessed.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to adjust to a new dental crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most patients find that the sensation of a new crown feeling different begins to settle within one to two weeks. Bite sensitivity, awareness of extra bulk, and minor changes in speech are all typical early experiences. The adaptation timeline can vary depending on the individual and the location of the crown within the mouth. Posterior crowns (back teeth) sometimes feel more intrusive initially due to their involvement in the chewing process. If symptoms have not improved after two weeks, a clinical review is advisable.

mainEntity.name: Can a dental crown be adjusted after it has been fitted?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Minor adjustments to a crown's biting surface can usually be made at a follow-up appointment. Your dentist will use articulating paper — a thin marking paper that records where the teeth make contact — to identify any high spots and selectively adjust the crown's surface. This is a routine and comfortable procedure. More significant fitting concerns, such as poor marginal adaptation or a crown that is too wide in profile, may require the crown to be remade. Your dentist will advise on the most appropriate course of action following examination.

mainEntity.name: Why do my gums feel sore around my new crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mild gum soreness around a new crown is common in the first few days following placement. The gum tissue may have been temporarily displaced during the impression-taking process, or may be responding to the new restoration at its margin. This usually settles with good oral hygiene. However, if gum soreness persists beyond two weeks, if there is swelling, bleeding on brushing, or a visible gap between the crown and gum, these findings should be evaluated by your dentist, as they may indicate a marginal fit issue or localised gum inflammation.

mainEntity.name: Could my crown be too wide because of a laboratory error?

acceptedAnswer.text: In some cases, a crown may not conform precisely to the intended measurements due to variations in the impression or scanning process, or during laboratory fabrication. However, this is not always the cause of a crown feeling wide. The sensation of width can also arise from natural adaptation differences, material dimensions, or gum tissue changes. The only reliable way to determine whether there is a genuine fitting issue is through a clinical assessment by your dentist, who can examine the crown margins, bite contact, and overall contour directly.

mainEntity.name: What happens if my dental crown does not fit correctly?

acceptedAnswer.text: If clinical assessment confirms that a crown does not fit correctly — whether due to poor marginal adaptation, an incorrect bite height, or inappropriate contour — your dentist will discuss the available options with you. In many cases, minor adjustments resolve the concern. Where the crown itself requires correction, it may need to be remade. This is not an uncommon situation in restorative dentistry and does not necessarily reflect poor clinical care. Treatment outcomes and decisions will always be based on your individual clinical presentation and discussed with you in full before any further work proceeds.
